extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or beginning graduate students in algebraic geometry (Math 216 readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Study and apply definitions, properties, and examples of normality, factoriality (UFD-ness), associated points/primes, and rational/total quotient rings in schemes and rings; includes exercises and propositions to check and use these concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is normal if all of its stalks OX,p are normal, i.e., are integral domains, and integrally closed in their fraction fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: since reducedness is a stalk-local property, normal schemes are reduced. Use Exercise 5.4.A and related remarks to check normality on affines and via localization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrally closed domains localize
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an integrally closed domain and S is a multiplicative subset not containing 0, then S^{-1}A is an integrally closed domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.4.A: prove by lifting an equation in the fraction field of S^{-1}A to A[x]; this fact lets one check normality on Spec A by checking stalks/localizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking normality for quasicompact schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: For quasicompact schemes, normality can be checked at closed points, since any point is a generization of a closed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exercise references (5.1.E and 5.4.A) — reduces pointwise checking to a smaller set (closed points) for quasicompact schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal schemes need not be integral
rubrics_metrics.description: Normality does not imply integrality: the disjoint union of two normal schemes is normal, e.g., Spec k ⊔ Spec k ≅ Spec(k × k) is normal, but its ring of global sections is not an integral domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of global vs. local distinctions: normal is a stalk-local property; global rings may fail to be domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian scheme normal decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian scheme is normal if and only if it is the finite disjoint union of integral Noetherian normal schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.4.B (marked 'UNIMPORTANT EXERCISE'): uses Exercise 5.3.C; useful to reduce to integral components in Noetherian setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent local/global integral closure (Proposition 5.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an integral domain A, the following are equivalent: (i) A is integrally closed; (ii) A_p is integrally closed for all prime ideals p ⊂ A; (iii) A_m is integrally closed for all maximal ideals m ⊂ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use localization-preservation of integral closure (Exercise 5.4.A) and the construction in the proof to reduce non-integral closure of A to some localization A_m that also fails to be integrally closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: Given s in the fraction field K(A), the ideal I := { r ∈ A : r s ∈ A } is the ideal of denominators of s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: I is an ideal; it need not be principal (see Exercise 5.4.D and later exercises). In good situations (Noetherian, normal) the ideal of denominators has codimension 1 behavior (Algebraic Hartogs’s Lemma 11.3.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial (locally) / definition of factorial scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is factorial if all the stalks of X are unique factorization domains (UFDs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes called 'locally factorial' (terminology caution); factorial implies normal, but the converse may fail. To show factoriality one can find an appropriate affine cover, but such a cover need not exist even if X is factorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization preserves UFD-ness
rubrics_metrics.description: Any nonzero localization of a unique factorization domain is a unique factorization domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.4.E: use this to deduce that if A is a UFD then Spec A is factorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical checks for UFD (methods list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to check that a Noetherian integral domain A is a UFD include: (0) elementary euclidean algorithm cases (Z, k[t], Z[i]); polynomial rings over a UFD via Gauss’s Lemma; (1) localization of a UFD is UFD; (2) height-1 primes are principal (Proposition 11.3.5); (3) A is normal and Cl(A)=0; (4) Nagata’s Lemma. Caution: A[[x]] need not be a UFD even when A is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Remark 5.4.6 for sources and cautions; these are practical tools rather than a single decisive test in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial implies normality
rubrics_metrics.description: Unique factorization domains are integrally closed; hence factorial schemes are normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.4.F (IMPORTANT EXERCISE): show UFD → integrally closed. Note examples demonstrating the converses can fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of normal schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical examples: A^n, P^n, Spec Z are normal. If A is integrally closed then A[x] is integrally closed (nontrivial fact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Exercise 5.4.G and references (Bourbaki, Eisenbud) for proofs. Exercise 5.4.I–L give more nuanced examples involving quadratic extensions and cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic extension normality criterion (exercise form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A is a UFD with 2 invertible and z^2 − f irreducible in A[z]. If f has no repeated prime factors then Spec A[z]/(z^2 − f) is normal; if f has repeated prime factors then it is not normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.4.H gives a constructive proof using expressing possible algebraic elements as g + h z and Gauss's lemma to study integrality over A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete normal/non-UFD examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Z[√−5] is integrally closed but not a UFD (Exercise 5.4.K). A = k[w,x,y,z]/(wz − xy) (the cone over a quadric surface) is integrally closed but not a UFD (Exercise 5.4.L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises provide hints: use grading arguments to show irreducibility of homogeneous elements and Gauss-type arguments for integrality; these serve as key counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: UFD-ness is not affine-local
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a UFD is not an affine-local property: a scheme can be covered by affine opens that are Spec of UFDs, yet the global ring A need not be a UFD (Exercise 5.4.N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete construction: the homogeneous degree 0 part of Q[x,y]_{x^2+y^2} gives such an example; number-theorists have Z[√−5] covered by D(2) and D(3) which are UFDs although Z[√−5] is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated points (geometric description) — property (A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The associated primes/points of an A-module M are precisely the generic points of irreducible components of the support of some element of M (on Spec A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This geometric viewpoint links 'fuzzy picture' intuition of nonreduced loci to algebra: associated points capture where 'levels of nonreducedness' or supports of sections concentrate (Exercise 5.5.A and following).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of associated points — property (B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian and M is finitely generated, then M has only a finite number of associated primes/points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.5.10(a) / Theorem 5.5.10(a). This is a Noetherian finiteness phenomenon; used to deduce that only finitely many irreducible closed subsets can be supports of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated points characterize zerodivisors — property (C)
rubrics_metrics.description: An element f of A is a zerodivisor on M (i.e., there exists m ≠ 0 with f m = 0) iff it vanishes at some associated point of M (i.e., is contained in some associated prime of M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One direction is immediate from definitions; use properties (A)–(B) and Theorem 5.5.10(c) to prove the equivalence and apply to detect zerodivisors geometrically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support of elements described by associated points
rubrics_metrics.description: Those subsets of Spec A which are the support of an element of M are exactly the closures of subsets of the associated points of M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.5.O and 5.5.P: construct sections supported exactly on a given associated prime; conversely, the support of an element is the closure of associated points where it has nonzero germ (Exercise 5.5.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization behavior of associated primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Association commutes with localization: for a multiplicative set S, Ass_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M) = { pS^{-1}A : p ∈ Ass_A M and p ∩ S = ∅ }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.5.F and Theorem 5.5.10(d): this shows associated primes are 'stalk-local' and can be checked on affines or distinguished opens; used to globalize associated points on schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injection into product of localizations at associated primes
rubrics_metrics.description: For M finitely generated over Noetherian A, the natural map M → ∏_{p ∈ Ass M} M_p is injective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as (5.5.3.1) and Theorem 5.5.10(b). Consequence: if a section/germ vanishes at all associated points, it is zero; useful to show schematic density and to control rational functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of associated prime (module-theoretic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prime p ⊂ A is associated to M if p is the annihilator of some element m ∈ M (i.e., p = Ann(m) = { a ∈ A : a m = 0 }).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, M has a submodule isomorphic to A/p. Denote the set by Ass M or Ass_A M (Section 5.5.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 5.5.10 (summary of properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian and M ≠ 0 is finitely generated, then (a) Ass M is finite and nonempty; (b) the map M → ⊕_{p∈Ass M} M_p is injective; (c) the set of zerodivisors of M equals ⋃_{p∈Ass M} p; (d) association commutes with localization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is proved via exercises (5.5.J–5.5.N). Use these parts when reasoning about supports, zerodivisors, and localization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational functions and maximal domain
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational function on a locally Noetherian scheme X is an element of the image of Γ(U, O_X) → ⊕_{p ∈ associated points in U} O_{X,p} for some open U containing all associated points; equivalently, a function defined on an open set containing all associated points. Each rational function has a maximal domain of definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 5.5.6: use injectivity (5.5.5.1) to see maximal domain exists; regular at p means p is in the maximal domain. Examples: on Spec k[x,y]/(y^2, xy) some fractions are rational, others are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total fraction (quotient) ring
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational functions on X form a ring, called the total fraction (quotient) ring of X (for affine X = Spec A, this is the total fraction ring of A). If X is integral this coincides with the function field K(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 5.5.7: provides a global notion extending K(X) to nonintegral schemes by inverting nonzerodivisors appropriately (i.e., by restriction to opens containing associated points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypersurfaces have no embedded points
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = k[x_1,...,x_n]/(f) with f nonzero, then A has no embedded associated primes (i.e., no embedded points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.5.I: hint uses UFD property of k[x_1,...,x_n] and common-factor arguments; useful when analyzing singular/nonreduced hypersurfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary decomposition and associated primes relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated primes of an ideal are precisely the radicals of the ideals appearing in any primary decomposition of that ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aside 5.5.13: primary ideals I with I : x^n ⊂ I for some n define primary decompositions; although not developed here, primary decomposition gives an explicit link between associated primes and components of supports.
